classification.difficultyReason: Translate the supplied quotient into a labelled secant diagram and explain how its gradient tends to the tangent gradient.

content.prompt:
[Revising the mechanics of the standard version]

The standard formula for differentiation by first principles is
$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.$$
Explain, using a clear diagram, how this formula finds the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $P(x,f(x))$.

answer.short: The secant through $P(x,f(x))$ and $Q(x+h,f(x+h))$ has gradient $\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$. As $h\to0$, $Q$ approaches $P$ and, when $f$ is differentiable at $x$, the secant gradient approaches the tangent gradient $f'(x)$.
answer.worked:
Choose a second point $Q(x+h,f(x+h))$ on the curve, with $h\ne0$.
$$\begin{align*}m_{PQ}&=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{(x+h)-x}\\m_{PQ}&=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.\end{align*}$$
The horizontal change is $h$ and the vertical change is $f(x+h)-f(x)$. As $h\to0$, $Q$ approaches $P$. When $f$ is differentiable at $x$, the secant approaches the tangent at $P$, so
$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.$$
The diagram illustrates a positive value of $h$.

spec.description: Authored illustrative curve, tangent at P and dashed secant through P and Q; horizontal and vertical changes are labelled. Source supplies no diagram.
spec.mathematics: The secant gradient is the vertical change divided by h; its limit is the tangent gradient when the derivative exists. Curve coordinates are illustrative, not additional givens.
